Messages.Author: Judith Cookson Grunberger
Messages.Body:
I bled my prey, and he had one of his minions react and play a telepathic
counter, thus reducing my puny bleed to zero. Then he decided that once
he had reduced the bleed, he also wanted to block and torpor my vampire
(arrrrrg, Tremere/Ventrue thaumaturgy/fortitude ... arrrrrrrrg).

Can he do this? I didn't think Telepathic Counter was meant that way. I
agree that it reduces the bleed, but doesn't that imply that you have let
the bleed through? I understand that a De-evolutionized Gangrel with a
zero bleed can be blocked (mine was not a Gangrel, btw), but can you
block after a Telepathic Counter?

It sucked. My vampire got toasted. Normally my deck works really well,
until you get it into a game where it is the only non-combat deck. Sigh.
But it clued me into the fact that Burst of Sunlight/Skin of Steel is a
pretty nifty combo.

So. Anyone got some insight? Tom?

Judy

Hi Judy,
If he used telepathic counter to reduce the bleed then the action
(bleeding) was unblocked, therefore no combat. If he had blocked you
instead of playing telepathic counter there still would have been no
bleed (the action was blocked) and he could have his way with your vampire.

>He could not get into the combat if he played the TC. It's not a bleed until

>the vamp deals the damage to the player and thus could not be reduced.
>Vamps ATTEMPT to bleed. A bleed can only be reduced once someone IS bled,
>which means that the action was unblocked. Sounds like your partner drew a good
>card and wanted to hose someone after playing the TC. Alas....He loses the
>argument.

Sorry - you can change the amount of a bleed before or after any/all
attempts to block. You can raise it with Conditioning or lower it with
TC. After someone plays TC, you could still raise it with Conditioning,
and they could still block (if you weren't careful to ask first):

A: I bleed you
B: I reduce the bleed by one with TC.
A: Do you block?
B: No.
A: I Bleed at +3 with conditioning: 1 + 3 - 1 = 3!

Reacting is separate from blocking. He wins the argument.

Tom has already made posts using the same logic I mimicked here.

As for the DT, the closest match is:

Subject: Revised Jyhad FAQ: 4/18/95 version
Date: 18 Apr 1995 23:01:44 GMT
Message-ID: <3n1gco$7...@darkstar.UCSC.EDU>

Q: Can you play a Reaction after your opponent plays an
Action Modifier, or only directly after they play the
Action? (Specific situation: Rob bleeds Roy. Roy
declines to block, but plays the reaction Telepathic
Counter. Rob plays the action modifier Conditioning. Roy
plays the reaction Telepathic Misdirection. Rob claims
that this is illegal, that Roy passed his chance to play
additional Reactions and so can't play one now.)
A: It is legal to play reaction cards both before and after action
modifiers.

-----
Note that the example spells out explicitly that Roy declined
to block before playing TC - so it doesn't help this arguemnet one
way or the other.

My reasoning is: the opportunity to block is not affected
by Reaction Cards that modify the bleed any more than it is
affected by Action Modifiers that modify the bleed.

Your reasoning is...?
--
-----

This actually has an analogy with Flesh of Marble. You can't prevent
damage until it happens (which is why FoM + 1 point damage prevention is
no good - you have to use the prevention first). Likewise one could argue
that you can reduce bleeds til they happen either. + bleed would have no
such restrictions.

Naturally the case that WotC wasn't being that precise in their
terminology is entirely plausible. It's not a common interpretation.

I don't play it that way - actually never even thought about it until
today. It actually would help Telepathic Counter a little as you can no
longer boost a bleed after the TC's been played.

Curt Adams (curt...@aol.com)

There is bleed that can be reduced even before there is an attempt to

IMO that means that you can reduce the acting minion's bleed before an

sjoh...@math.scarolina.edu (L. Scott Johnson) writes:

>Sorry - you can change the amount of a bleed before or after any/all

>TC. After someone plays TC, you could still raise it with Conditioning,
>and they could still block (if you weren't careful to ask first):

>A: I bleed you
>B: I reduce the bleed by one with TC.
>A: Do you block?
>B: No.
>A: I Bleed at +3 with conditioning: 1 + 3 - 1 = 3!

>Reacting is separate from blocking. He wins the argument.

So basically what this is all about is that the person who plays TC
can play it before she decides whether she wants to block or not. This
was the hard part for me also because we usually play TC _after_
decision not to block.

However, if the palyer says that the bleed goes through and then plays
TC she cannot back out and block afterwards. This is because the rules
say that after a player has passed the opportunity to block, she
cannot block the same action anymore. She has an opportunity to
block after TC has been played, but not after deciding not to block.
